    *   "Queens separated by more than one row MAY share a long diagonal; this is not the ordinary chess N-queens diagonal rule." This is a crucial distinction. Standard N-queens forbids any two queens on the same diagonal (slope $\pm 1$). Here, only queens in *consecutive* rows cannot be on adjacent columns. So, $(r, c)$ and $(r+2, c+2)$ are allowed to touch diagonally? No, wait.
    *   Let's re-read carefully: "Queens may not touch, including diagonally." This usually means the 8 neighbors of a square.

This implies that if I have queens at $(1, 1)$ and $(3, 3)$, they are on the same diagonal but don't touch. They are allowed. The constraint is strictly local: no touching neighbors. So, $|c_i - c_{i+1}| \neq 0$ (same column) and $|c_i - c_{i+1}| \neq 1$ (touching diagonally).
    *   Wait, standard N-queens also forbids same column ($|c_i - c_j| = 0$ for $i \neq j$). The rule "one in every row, every column" covers this.
